name: Tokenization
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Turning Anything Into a Token: The Practice of Tokenization
lesson.summary: Tokenization is the process of representing an asset, whether a currency unit, a share of a company, a piece of real estate, or a unique collectible, as a digital token on a blockchain, so that ownership and transfer of that asset can be tracked using the same ledger tools built for cryptocurrency.
lesson.body:
A token, covered earlier in this book, is a digital unit of value recorded and transferred on a blockchain, and a fungible token is a type of token where every unit is interchangeable and identical in value to every other unit, the way one dollar bill is worth exactly the same as any other dollar bill. Tokenization is the broader practice built on both of those ideas, taking something, whether purely digital or drawn from the physical world, and issuing a blockchain token that represents a claim on it or a right to it.

Tokenization takes two basic shapes, corresponding to the two kinds of tokens covered earlier. Fungible tokenization represents divisible, interchangeable value, for example a stablecoin where each token represents a claim on one dollar held somewhere, or a token representing one share in a pooled fund, where any unit is worth exactly the same as any other unit of the same token. Non-fungible tokenization represents a unique, non-interchangeable item, for example a token representing title to one specific property, or ownership of one particular piece of art, where each token is distinct and not simply interchangeable with another token of the same type.

The appeal of tokenizing an asset is that the asset then inherits the properties of whatever blockchain the token lives on. Transfers can settle as quickly as that chain confirms transactions, ownership records become visible and auditable by anyone able to read the chain rather than locked inside one institution's private database, and the token can typically be split into much smaller fractional units far more easily than the underlying asset itself could be divided. Tokenizing a commercial building, for instance, lets many separate investors each hold a small fractional token representing partial ownership, rather than requiring any single buyer to purchase the entire property outright.

The catch is that a blockchain token can only ever be as trustworthy as the real world process connecting it to whatever it claims to represent. The ledger can reliably guarantee that a token moved correctly from one wallet to another, since that is exactly the kind of fact a blockchain's consensus mechanism is built to verify. It cannot, on its own, guarantee that a stablecoin issuer actually holds the dollars its tokens claim to represent, or that a government deed registry recognizes a token holder as the asset's legal owner. That linkage depends entirely on a legal agreement, a custodian, or an auditor, none of which are enforced by the blockchain itself, only referenced by it.

A concrete illustration brings this together. A real estate tokenization project might issue tokens that each represent a fractional ownership interest in a specific rental property, letting those tokens trade freely on an exchange while a separate legal entity actually holds title to the building and distributes rental income to whoever holds the tokens at the time. The trading and record keeping move on-chain, exactly as the on-chain versus off-chain distinction from earlier in this section would predict, but the underlying legal and custodial trust relationship that makes the token meaningful in the first place remains firmly off-chain.
